passage: Monday: Gopika couldn't sleep. The news had shown whole villages in a far-off state under brown water, a girl her age carrying a goat on her shoulders. "Why do we just watch?" she asked her mother, Sangeeta, angry and close to tears. Wednesday: The school eco club had a tree-planting drive on the bare hillside behind the stadium. The forest officer explained how roots hold soil so rain doesn't rush down all at once. Gopika dug three holes, her hands blistered, and felt the knot in her stomach loosen a little. Saturday: She set up a collection box outside the canteen for flood relief, with a sign she'd painted herself. "It's small," she told Sangeeta. "But it's something."

qa.q: How many holes did Gopika dig?
qa.a: Gopika dug three holes.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she asked, 'Why do we just watch?'
qa.a: She felt angry and upset, overwhelmed by the suffering of people far away and frustrated at feeling helpless.

qa.q: What turning point helped Gopika turn worry into action?
qa.a: Learning from the forest officer how roots hold soil made her see a link to the floods, and she acted by planting and then setting up a collection box.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see her daughter's week?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel worried at first by Gopika's distress but proud to see it turn into planting trees and a relief box.

grounding: Across a week a teenager worries about far-away flood victims, joins a tree planting and starts a relief box, as she grasps how the world is linked.

passage: Sumit, sit. You asked why I plant a tree every monsoon. When I was fifteen, the river near our town flooded the villages downstream. We were safe on the hill. But I saw the boats bringing people with nothing, children wrapped in sacks. I couldn't eat for two days. I kept asking why. Our science teacher took us up the ghat and showed us the stumps where the forest had been cut. "Rain runs off bare slopes like off a roof," she said. That Sunday I went with the college boys to plant saplings, the only girl in the group. My hands bled. Some saplings died. But I kept going every year. Your Urmila Dadi has planted fifty-eight trees. And I still think about those children.

qa.q: How old was Urmila when the river flooded the villages downstream?
qa.a: Fifteen.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel after seeing the boats bring people with nothing?
qa.a: She was so upset she couldn't eat for two days and kept asking why, showing deep concern for strangers she had never met.

qa.q: What turning point turned Urmila's worry into action?
qa.a: The teacher showing the cut stumps on the ghat helped her see how bare slopes cause floods, and she chose to start planting saplings.

qa.q: What might Sumit take away from Urmila Dadi's story?
qa.a: Sumit might see that caring for people far away can lead to steady small actions, like planting a tree every monsoon.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenage girl, concern for flood victims downstream led her to plant trees once she understood how deforestation causes floods.

passage: The tree-planting drive started at seven, but by ten the sun was brutal and there were only forty saplings for sixty volunteers. Vijay, sixteen, wiped his face with his T-shirt. On his phone that morning he'd seen photos of a coastal town in another country, houses gone, people sleeping on a school roof. He'd felt sick and angry. What was the point of a few trees here? He said so to Sarita, the volunteer coordinator. She handed him a sapling. "Mangroves on coasts, forests on hills, all the same story. Less heat, fewer floods. Every place connected." Vijay dug slowly, thinking about that. Then he asked for her number: the school holidays were coming, and he wanted to join the mangrove drive.

qa.q: How many saplings were there for sixty volunteers?
qa.a: Only forty saplings.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after seeing the photos of the coastal town?
qa.a: He felt sick and angry, and wondered if his few trees here could make any difference.

qa.q: What turning point changed Vijay's view of his work?
qa.a: Sarita explained how forests and mangroves everywhere reduce heat and floods, so Vijay saw the connection and chose to join the mangrove drive too.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Vijay's frustrated question?
qa.a: Sarita probably sees it as real concern, not laziness, and uses it as a chance to explain how places are linked.

grounding: A teenager planting trees feels anxious about far-off flood victims and grows wider concern as he learns how the world is connected.

passage:
At seven on Sunday morning, the mud along the creek in Mumbai smelled of salt and rot. Raghav, fifteen, was knee-deep in it, planting mangrove saplings with his friend Hemant and thirty other volunteers.
"Why mangroves, though?" Hemant grumbled, slapping a mosquito. "Trees are trees."
"They hold the mud when the sea pushes in," Raghav said. "Our geography sir showed us. Where they cut them, the floods come in worse."
He was thinking about the news from last week: a family in a far-off state sitting on their roof, water all around, an old man holding a radio above his head. Raghav had never been there. But he'd lain awake thinking of that man.
"It's not the same sea," Hemant said.
"Same world, though." Raghav pressed the soil around another sapling. "Everything's connected. The weather, the water. I can't fix that roof. I can do this."

qa.q: What was Raghav planting?
qa.a: Mangrove saplings.

qa.q: Why had Raghav lain awake after seeing the news?
qa.a: He was worried about the flooded family and the old man holding the radio, even though they were strangers far away.

qa.q: What choice has Raghav made about his worry, and why does it make sense to him?
qa.a: He turned it into planting mangroves, because he understands that protecting the coast helps against floods, and it is something he can actually do.

qa.q: How does Hemant seem to see the planting drive at first?
qa.a: Hemant sees it as muddy, mosquito-bitten work with no clear link to far-off floods, until Raghav explains how the world is connected.

grounding: It shows a teenager who joins a mangrove-planting drive and worries about strangers suffering from floods far away, his concern widening as he learns how the world is linked.

passage:
"Ammi, can I go for the tree-planting on Sunday? Jagdish Uncle is taking the building kids to the hill."
"At six in the morning? My daughter can't even wake up for school at seven."
"This is different." Afreen sat at the dining table. "And I want to collect old clothes too, for the flood villages in the north."
Abbu looked up from the newspaper. "Those villages are two thousand kilometres away, beta."
"So? The people are still real." Afreen's voice wobbled. "There was a girl my age in the photo, holding her little brother above the water. I keep thinking about her."
Ammi and Abbu looked at each other.
"And the trees?" Abbu asked, more gently.
"Our science teacher said forests on hills slow the rain going down into rivers. Hills everywhere. It's all connected."
Ammi sighed. "Fine. I'll set an alarm. And the clothes, take your brother's old jackets. He's grown out of all of them."

qa.q: What did Ammi say Afreen could take for the clothes collection?
qa.a: Her brother's old jackets.

qa.q: Why did Afreen's voice wobble when she spoke about the flood villages?
qa.a: She was upset and moved by the photo of a girl her age holding her brother above the water, and she couldn't stop thinking about her.

qa.q: What turning point changed her parents' response, and why?
qa.a: When Afreen explained the girl in the photo and how hill forests slow the rain into rivers, her parents saw her concern was real and informed, so they agreed.

qa.q: How might Abbu's view of Afreen change during this talk?
qa.a: He starts by pointing out the distance but grows gentler, perhaps seeing that his daughter cares for strangers and understands how things are linked.

passage:
Dear Wasim,
We did the tree-planting drive on Sunday! Two hundred saplings along the canal near our school. My hands are still full of blisters and I'm weirdly proud of them.
But I keep thinking about your last letter. The river in your town rising so fast, your neighbours' houses under water, the school closed for two weeks. I saw the news too. People I'll never meet, sitting on rooftops.
Our teacher explained how cutting forests upstream makes floods worse downstream. It made me feel angry and also kind of helpless. I planted my forty trees and thought: is this even anything?
But maybe it's how it starts. My trees here. Your river there. It's all one river, somehow.
Write back and tell me you're safe.
Manjula

qa.a: Two hundred saplings.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel after the teacher's explanation?
qa.a: Manjula felt angry and a bit helpless, worried about people far away in the floods.

qa.q: What could Manjula do next with this concern?
qa.a: Manjula could keep joining drives, learn more about how places are linked, and maybe help collect things for flood-hit families.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Wasim might feel cared about and less alone, knowing someone far away is thinking of Wasim's town.

passage:
Farhan, you asked me for the school radio what got me into the mangrove project. I'm Yamini, Class 10.
It started with a video. A fisherman's family on the coast, their hut half washed away after a storm surge. The father said the mangroves used to protect them, and they'd been cut for a hotel. I couldn't stop thinking about his daughter. She looked my age.
So when the eco-club said they were planting mangroves at the creek, I signed up. It was muddy and smelly and I loved it.
But honestly, sometimes I feel angry. And anxious. Like the problems are so big and I'm so small. Some nights I read news until I feel sick.
Then I think of the forty saplings I planted. Somewhere, one of them is growing. That helps.

qa.a: The mangroves.

qa.q: What does Yamini feel when reading news at night?
qa.a: Yamini feels angry and anxious, overwhelmed by how big the problems are.

qa.q: What could help Yamini when the worry gets too big?
qa.a: Yamini could limit night-time news, keep doing hands-on work like planting, and talk to a teacher or family about the worry.

qa.q: How might the fisherman's daughter feel if she knew about the mangrove project?
qa.a: She might feel seen and hopeful, knowing someone far away cares about people like her family.

"Madhav, you ask why your old Dada plants a tree every monsoon. It started when I was fifteen.
I, Rafiq, was in Class 10 in Patna when the Kosi floods hit north Bihar. I saw pictures in the newspaper of families on rooftops, children holding goats. I didn't know anyone there, but I couldn't sleep. I kept thinking, where will they go?
Our science teacher explained that cutting forests upstream makes floods worse. It made me angry. Why should poor farmers suffer for trees cut far away?
That month I joined the school tree-planting drive. We planted two hundred saplings along the river. It felt tiny. But it was something.
I still worry about people far away. Now I plant, and I send what I can when floods come."

The tree-planting drive started at six on Sunday, and it was pouring. Only eight students from Urmila's Class 11 showed up at the empty plot in Pune.
Urmila, sixteen, dug in the mud while her friend Vikas held the umbrella over the saplings. "Why do you even care so much?"
She wiped rain off her face. "Remember the news about the floods in Assam? A girl my age lost her house. I keep thinking about her."
"But you don't know her."
"So? If trees help keep the soil and the rain in place, I want to plant them. It's all connected."
Vikas grumbled, but he stayed until the last sapling was in. Urmila's hands were blistered. She felt tired and angry about the floods, and somehow better.

passage:
Kiran came home from the school eco-club meeting in their Bengaluru flat with muddy shoes and a list. "Rukmini Aunty," she told the neighbour on the landing, "we planted forty saplings near the lake today."
"Well done, Kiran. Why the long face then?"
Kiran leaned on the railing. "In class we learned about the floods in Kerala. Families lost everything. I keep seeing a video of an old man carrying his cat through water. I don't know him, but I can't stop thinking about him."
Rukmini Aunty nodded. "It's heavy to care about people you'll never meet."
"Is it silly?"
"No. It means you understand we're all tied together. Just don't carry it alone."
Kiran smiled a little and went in to write the next club poster.

qa.a: They planted forty saplings.

qa.q: Why did Kiran have a long face after the eco-club meeting?
qa.a: She was worried and sad about flood victims in Kerala, especially the old man with his cat, even though she didn't know him.

qa.a: She tells Kiran not to carry the worry alone, so her wide concern stays healthy and she can keep acting on it.

qa.q: How does Rukmini Aunty see Kiran's worry?
qa.a: She sees it as a sign that Kiran understands how people are tied together, not as silly.

Kamal pressed the earth down with both palms. 'Did you see the floods on the news? A whole village school was under water. Kids our age were on rooftops.'
'That's far from here, yaar.'
'That's the thing. Sir said last week the rivers and forests are all connected: cut trees in one place, soil washes away, floods get worse somewhere else. So maybe it's not that far.'
'You think one neem is going to stop a flood?'
'No.' Kamal wiped his forehead, leaving a streak of mud. 'But I keep thinking about those kids. I can't do nothing. This is something.'
Mohit was quiet, then picked up the second sapling. 'Okay. Show me how deep.'

passage: It was the pictures Urmila sent in August that got to me. We became pen friends through a school exchange, and her village near the Kosi floods almost every monsoon. That month her whole courtyard was brown water, and her little brother's school books were drying on the roof. I'm Simran, and I live in a dry flat in Jaipur; I had never thought about rain as something that takes things away. So when our eco-club announced a tree-planting drive along the city's dry riverbed, I signed up first. Our teacher explained how bare slopes let rain run off faster and how rivers carry that water far. I know my forty saplings won't save Urmila's courtyard. But planting them felt less like charity and more like admitting we are on the same map. I still text her before every monsoon.

qa.q: What was drying on the roof in Urmila's pictures?
qa.a: Her little brother's school books.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when the August pictures came?
qa.a: Simran felt shaken and worried for Urmila, and uneasy at never having thought of rain as something that takes things away.

qa.q: What else could Simran do that would help Urmila's family more directly?
qa.a: Simran could ask the eco-club teacher about a proper flood-relief collection, and keep listening to what Urmila says the family actually needs.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel getting Simran's texts before every monsoon?
qa.a: Urmila may feel remembered and less alone, knowing someone in a dry city thinks about the family's home when the rains come 🤍

Ankita arrived early and planted more saplings than anyone, but she was quiet, not her usual self. During the water break she showed me a photo on her phone of a flooded town down the coast and asked, 'Will our trees ever matter to people there?' I explained, simply, how forests hold soil and slow rainwater, and that one drive is small but not nothing. She listened, then said she felt guilty having a dry bedroom. Her friend Nandini suggested a stall at the school fair for flood relief. Ankita brightened and started listing what they could sell. Action: on Monday I will connect them with the school's relief committee, and I will check in with Ankita, as her worry seemed heavy.

passage:
15 August, night
Flag hoisting in the morning, then the colony tree drive. Yash and I planted three neem saplings by the drain road, muddy up to our elbows. Aunty from B-block said, "Why bother, the municipality will cut them." I watered them anyway.
Then tonight on the news, the floods up north. A whole village under water, people on rooftops with their goats. I don't know anyone there. But I can't stop thinking about them. Same rain, same sky, and our drains are choked with plastic too. It all feels connected and too big, and I'm angry that grown-ups just shrug.
Tomorrow I'll ask Sir if our class can collect clothes for the relief drive. And I'll check on the neems.
Alka
